1:
The inscription differs from its neighbours, and Delitzsch makes that the key. It is the only song of degrees whose title uses the preposition rather than the article; a Jewish commentary makes it a song upon the steps by which God leads the righteous into the other world, and those who explain the degrees of pilgrimage count the unique form in their favour. Delitzsch takes the particle instead for the one that marks a rule, so that the psalm is composed after the manner of steps; and against the pilgrim reading he sets the opening, which implies a fixed abode far from the singer's native mountains. Clarke reads it as a prayer of the Jews in captivity, and adds a structure nobody else proposes: a dialogue in which the worshipper speaks the first two verses, the priest answers with the third, the worshipper replies with the fourth but seems to doubt whether he will be heard, and the priest resumes at the fifth.

Whether the first line is a statement or a question divides them. Ellicott is most decided: our version is incorrect in following the Greek and Latin in making whence a relative, since the Hebrew word is always interrogative; but the margin is hardly right either in making the whole verse a question. He renders it, I will lift up mine eyes to the hills — whence comes my help? — the question being not one of doubt but put for the sake of the emphatic answer. Henry uses the interrogative reading against creature confidence: shall I depend on princes and great men, who like hills fill the earth and hold up their heads toward heaven? We must lift our eyes above them, looking beyond instruments to God who makes them what they are to us.

Which hills are meant is disputed along the same line. Wesley says Zion and Moriah; Henry agrees, taking them for the hills on which the temple stood; Gill offers the same, or heaven itself, and denies that the psalmist is scanning Judea for men coming to help. Ellicott leaves the standpoint undecided — the poet may have been turning toward the mountains of Israel from Mesopotamia, or near the end of a pilgrim journey — and adds what the mountains meant besides: a barrier of defence, and heights from which to watch for the messengers of peace. Augustine allegorises them into the apostles and the Scriptures, and presses the distinction: the help is from him of whose fulness the hills received, not from the hills.

Calvin alone finds the opening line awkward and answers his own objection. The writer, he says, seems at first to speak in the person of an unbelieving man; since God prevents his people with his blessings, they cast their eyes directly upon him, whereas here the prophet looks unsettledly now this way and now that, as if faith did not direct him. His answer is that the thoughts of the godly are never so stayed on the word as not to be carried away at the first impulse: inclined to the earth, we can scarcely help being moved by the enticements before us. All are prone to be cheated; but Satan bewitches unbelievers with his enchantments, while in believers God corrects the vice of their nature. Though every help in the world should offer itself, we ought to seek safety nowhere but in God.

Spurgeon reads the verse through the geography of health. Dwellers in valleys are subject to disorders for which there is no cure but a sojourn in the uplands; below, they are the prey of marauders, and the surest escape is to fly to the mountain strongholds. He then names the hills he means — the purposes of God, the divine attributes, the immutable promises, the covenant ordered and sure — and warns that Satan will try to keep our eyes on our sorrows.
2:
The answer turns on a title. Ellicott points out that the help comes not, as Canaanite superstition said, from the sacred summits but from their Creator, and makes a dating argument of the phrase, maker of heaven and earth being a peculiarity of psalms certainly after the exile. When the idolater pointed to his visible god and taunted the Israelite with having none, the natural reply was that his God made the heavens. Gill turns the title into an argument from ability: what can he not do, who has made both?

The third verse is disputed as to mood. Ellicott says the Greek and Latin rightly render it may he not suffer thy foot to be moved, since the Hebrew cannot be a simple negative, and takes the next verse to prove that Israel is addressed. Gill reads it as an address to the psalmist's own soul or to a friend: the saints may be moved in some sense, their feet almost gone and their steps well nigh slipped, but not so as to fall finally. Clarke makes it a matter of standing ground: the foundation of God's power cannot be moved, and while a man stands on it neither can his foot.

The sleepless keeper draws in the classics. Gill grants the appearance against it: God may seem to sleep when he withdraws his presence and defers help, but does not in reality sleep, nor even slumber. He sets beside the verse Homer's Jupiter, not held by sleep while gods and men sleep all night. Clarke makes God a watchman who guards the city through the night-watches and is never overtaken by drowsiness, and quotes as its counterpart a Greek tragedy on the god whose eyes all-subduing sleep never closes. Ellicott is interested in the form: the repetition with an added synonym is a good instance of the step-like style that many suppose gives these psalms their name, though there is no climax between the two words, the first being if anything the stronger, since it is used of the sleep of death.

On the keeper Ellicott continues the formal observation — the prominent word is caught up from the preceding verse, amplified, repeated and amplified again — and calls the change to preserve in the closing verses an unfortunate substitution. On the shade at the right hand he rejects as prosaic the attempt to make it the sunny southern side, preferring a confusion of metaphors with the figure of the right-hand comrade in war. Delitzsch keeps to the shadow, an overshadowing that spreads over the man and screens him from the sun's heat, and notes what the poet does: applying believingly to himself, as one among God's people, what holds good of the Keeper of Israel. Gill gives the keeper a name: Christ, appointed by the Father and consented to by those who commit their souls to him.

The sun and moon are read at three levels. Clarke gives the Chaldee, which turns them into morning spectres under the sun's government and nocturnal spectres under the moon's, then sets it aside: the psalmist means no sun-stroke by day nor frost-bite by night. Ellicott canvasses the moon. There may be an allusion to the old belief in the harmful influence of moonlight, still recalled in the word lunacy; others set the cold of the night against the noonday heat, the impression that intense cold burns being common in the East; or the harmful effects of night air may be meant. Wesley takes the second without hesitation — the moon's cold and moisture — adding that intemperate heats and colds are the springs of many diseases. On the last promises Gill distinguishes what the keeping does not cover from what it does: not exemption from affliction, but preservation from the dominion of sin, from the lusts of the world, and from sinking under the temptations of the evil one.
